blocks.text: In a crash test a dummy slams into an airbag and slows from 14 m/s to rest. Without the airbag the head stops in a few milliseconds; with it, in about a tenth of a second. The change in momentum is the same, yet the peak force is lower by a factor of more than ten. Impulse-momentum links force, duration and velocity change directly.

blocks.markdown: Newton's second law can be written in terms of **linear momentum** $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$ (kg m/s): $\sum\mathbf F=d\mathbf p/dt$. Integrating over a time interval gives a result that needs no acceleration: the **impulse** of the net force, $\int\mathbf F\,dt$ (N s), equals the change in momentum. This is especially powerful when forces act for a short time and vary in a complicated way, as in collisions, impacts and explosions.

blocks.title: Impulse and momentum
blocks.text: Linear momentum is $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$. The linear impulse of a force over $t_1\to t_2$ is $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\mathbf F\,dt$, the area under the force-time graph. 1 N s = 1 kg m/s.

blocks.caption: The linear impulse-momentum principle: initial momentum plus impulse equals final momentum. It is a vector equation; apply it along each axis.

blocks.title: Time-varying force
blocks.prompt: A 50 kg cart on a smooth horizontal track is moving at 2.0 m/s when a force $F=120t-20t^2$ (N, $t$ in s) acts in the direction of motion from $t=0$ to $t=4$ s. Find the cart's velocity at $t=4$ s.

steps.text: Apply impulse-momentum in the direction of motion.

blocks.answer: The cart's velocity at $t=4$ s is about 12.7 m/s.

blocks.markdown: When there is **no external impulse** on a system of particles over the interval (the external forces are zero, or negligible compared with the large internal forces acting briefly), the total linear momentum of the system is conserved. The internal forces between the particles cancel in pairs by Newton's third law, so they cannot change the total momentum. This applies component by component: a force in the vertical direction does not prevent horizontal momentum from being conserved.

blocks.caption: Conservation of linear momentum, valid when the external impulse on the system is zero or negligible.

blocks.title: Recoil of a rifle
blocks.prompt: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 15 g bullet horizontally at a muzzle velocity of 800 m/s relative to the ground. Treat the rifle as free to recoil. Find the recoil velocity.

steps.text: Initial momentum of the rifle and bullet is zero. Take the bullet's direction as positive.

blocks.answer: The rifle recoils at 3.0 m/s opposite to the bullet.

rows: Short, large force; interaction time known
External force acts for a long time
blocks.caption: Choosing an approach.

blocks.markdown: **Average force during a collision.** In an impact the contact force may be huge and varies unpredictably, but its time integral equals the momentum change, which is easy to find. Dividing by the contact time $\Delta t$ gives the **average force**. The peak force is always larger than the average. Stretching the contact time reduces the average force for the same momentum change.

blocks.title: Average force on a ball
blocks.prompt: A 0.057 kg ball approaches a wall at 30 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 24 m/s. The ball is in contact with the wall for 5.0 ms. Find the average force on the ball.

steps.text: Take the rebound direction as positive: initial velocity is $-30$ m/s, final is $+24$ m/s.
Average force from impulse over the contact time.

blocks.answer: The wall exerts an average force of about 616 N on the ball, directed away from the wall.

items: Define a positive direction for each axis and write signed velocities.
Draw the interaction as 'before' and 'after' with all external forces listed.
Decide whether the external impulse is negligible (conserve momentum) or must be included.
Apply $\sum m\mathbf v_1+\int\sum\mathbf F\,dt=\sum m\mathbf v_2$ per axis.
Convert units: grams to kg, milliseconds to seconds.

blocks.title: Reversals and external forces
blocks.text: A rebound reverses the sign of the velocity, so the change in momentum is the sum of the two speeds, not their difference. Momentum conservation fails along any direction in which a significant external force (gravity over a long interval, a fixed support) acts.

points: The linear impulse-momentum principle is $m\mathbf v_1+\int\mathbf F\,dt=m\mathbf v_2$; impulse is the area under the force-time curve in N s.
With negligible external impulse, total momentum is conserved, giving the recoil of a gun: $m_rv_r=-m_bv_b$.
Average impact force is $F_{avg}=\Delta p/\Delta t$; increasing contact time lowers the force for the same momentum change.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a valid unit for impulse?

distractorRationale.c: Correct: force times time; equals kg m/s.

questions.explanation: Impulse is force multiplied by time, so its SI unit is N s, which is dimensionally the same as the momentum unit kg m/s. The other options are the units of energy or moment, power and force.

questions.stem: An airbag reduces injury during a crash mainly because it

options.text: Cancels the impulse of the crash
Increases the time over which the occupant's momentum changes, reducing the average force

questions.correctOptionText: Increases the time over which the occupant's momentum changes, reducing the average force

distractorRationale.a: The occupant still stops, so the momentum change is the same.
distractorRationale.c: The impulse equals the momentum change and cannot be avoided.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: $F_{avg}=\Delta p/\Delta t$ with larger $\Delta t$.

questions.explanation: The momentum change of the occupant is fixed by the speed to be lost. By lengthening the stopping time, the airbag lowers the average force.

questions.stem: A freely recoiling cannon on smooth horizontal ground fires a shell horizontally. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The total horizontal momentum of cannon and shell is conserved
The momentum of the cannon alone is conserved
The kinetic energy of cannon and shell is conserved
The shell and cannon gain equal speeds

questions.correctOptionText: The total horizontal momentum of cannon and shell is conserved

distractorRationale.a: Correct: no external horizontal impulse acts.
distractorRationale.b: The cannon receives an impulse from the shell's expulsion, so its own momentum changes.
distractorRationale.c: The explosion adds chemical energy, so kinetic energy increases.
distractorRationale.d: Equal and opposite momenta, but different masses, mean different speeds.

questions.explanation: The internal force from the propellant acts equally and oppositely on shell and cannon, and no horizontal external impulse acts, so the system's horizontal momentum stays zero. Their momenta are equal and opposite; the lighter one moves faster.

questions.stem: A force pulse rises linearly from zero to a peak of 800 N and falls linearly back to zero in a total time of 0.020 s. The impulse delivered is

distractorRationale.c: Treats the pulse as a rectangle of peak height.
distractorRationale.d: Forgets to use seconds and multiplies instead.

questions.explanation: The impulse is the area under the force-time graph, a triangle of base 0.020 s and height 800 N. Its area is $\tfrac12(0.020)(800)=8.0$ N s.

questions.stem: A 70 kg person standing in a 30 kg boat initially at rest on still water jumps horizontally at 3.0 m/s relative to the boat. Neglecting water resistance, the boat's speed immediately after the jump is

distractorRationale.a: Treats the boat as infinitely light or ignores momentum conservation.
distractorRationale.b: Takes 3.0 m/s as a ground speed shared by the mass ratio, $3.0(30)/70=1.3$ m/s.
distractorRationale.d: This is the person's speed relative to the water.

questions.explanation: Momentum about the water is zero, so $70(3.0-v_b)-30v_b=0$, because the person's ground velocity is the relative velocity minus the boat's backward speed. Hence $210=100v_b$ and $v_b=2.1$ m/s.

questions.stem: A 30 kg crate on a smooth horizontal floor starts from rest and is pushed by a force that increases uniformly as $F=200t$ (N, $t$ in s). Find its speed at $t=3.0$ s in m/s.
questions.explanation: The impulse is $\int_0^3200t\,dt=100(9)=900$ N s. Then $30v=900$, giving $v=30$ m/s.

questions.stem: A 0.145 kg baseball arrives at 38 m/s and leaves the bat in the opposite direction at 45 m/s. The contact lasts 1.2 ms. Find the average force on the ball in newtons.
questions.explanation: The momentum change is $0.145(45+38)=12.04$ N s because the velocity reverses. Dividing by 0.0012 s gives $F_{avg}=10\,030$ N, about 10 kN.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg gun on smooth ground fires a 10 kg shell horizontally. The muzzle velocity is 500 m/s relative to the gun barrel. Find the recoil speed of the gun in m/s.
questions.explanation: Let the recoil speed be $v_g$. The shell's ground velocity is $500-v_g$, and zero initial momentum gives $10(500-v_g)=1500v_g$. Then $5000=1510v_g$ and $v_g=3.31$ m/s.

questions.stem: Derive the linear impulse-momentum principle from Newton's second law and explain how it is used to estimate the average force in a collision of known duration. Discuss why increasing the contact time reduces the force.
markingGuide: Multiply by $dt$ and integrate from $t_1$ to $t_2$: $\int\mathbf F\,dt=m\mathbf v_2-m\mathbf v_1$.
Define impulse as the time integral of force, the area under the force-time graph.
Average force $F_{avg}=\Delta p/\Delta t$ using the measured momentum change and contact time.
For a fixed $\Delta p$, a larger $\Delta t$ gives smaller $F_{avg}$ (airbags, crumple zones, bending knees).
questions.explanation: The principle is just the integrated form of Newton's second law. Because it relates force and time to velocity change, it handles impacts without knowing the detailed force history.

questions.stem: State the condition under which the linear momentum of a system of particles is conserved and use it to explain the recoil of a gun. Explain why the lighter body gets the greater share of the kinetic energy.
markingGuide: Total momentum is conserved when there is no external impulse in that direction over the interval.
Internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs, so their impulses cancel.
Gun and projectile start at rest so $m_gv_g+m_pv_p=0$ and the gun recoils opposite to the projectile.
$|v_g|=m_pv_p/m_g$, so the heavier gun moves slower.
Kinetic energy $p^2/2m$ with equal momentum magnitudes means the lighter body has the larger kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite momenta follow from conservation. Since $T=p^2/(2m)$, the same momentum carried by a lighter mass means more kinetic energy.
